section.title: Against the Mountains of Israel
section.sectionRationale: The first spoken oracle of the book turns not to the city but to the land itself, the mountains, hills, ravines, and valleys where Israel built her high places. God sets His face against the very hilltop shrines the people trusted, promising to strew them with the corpses of their own worshipers, yet He also promises to leave a remnant who will remember Him and loathe their idolatry.
section.thesis: God will demolish every high place where Israel exchanged His worship for idols, executing judgment on the land itself, yet even this devastation is aimed at a remnant who will at last know that He is the LORD and turn from the idols that ruined them.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the oracle against the mountains and their high places; the slain lying among their own idols, and the survivors scattered to the nations who will remember and loathe themselves; and the summary word, the land made desolate until all know that the LORD has spoken.

units.label: Set your face against the mountains

verses.text: And the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, set your face against the mountains of Israel and prophesy against them.

You are to say: ‘O mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord GOD! This is what the Lord GOD says to the mountains and hills, to the ravines and valleys: I am about to bring a sword against you, and I will destroy your {{bamot|high places}}.
Your altars will be demolished and your incense altars will be smashed; and I will cast down your slain before your idols.
I will lay the corpses of the Israelites before their idols and scatter your bones around your altars.

Wherever you live, the cities will be laid waste and the high places will be demolished, so that your altars will be laid waste and desecrated, your idols smashed and obliterated, your incense altars cut down, and your works blotted out.
The slain will fall among you, and {{yada_yhwh|you will know that I am the LORD}}.

units.label: A remnant who will remember and loathe themselves
units.note: scattered among the nations, yet not forgotten

verses.text: Yet I will leave a remnant, for some of you will escape the sword when you are scattered among the nations and throughout the lands.

Then in the nations to which they have been carried captive, your survivors will remember Me, how I have been grieved by their adulterous hearts that turned away from Me, and by their eyes that lusted after idols. So they will loathe themselves for the evil they have done and for all their abominations.
And they will know that I am the LORD; I did not declare in vain that I would bring this calamity upon them.

units.label: The land made desolate until all know the LORD
units.note: clapping in mourning, then knowledge of God

verses.text: This is what the Lord GOD says: Clap your hands, stomp your feet, and cry out “Alas!” because of all the wicked abominations of the house of Israel, who will fall by sword and famine and plague.
He who is far off will die by the plague, he who is near will fall by the sword, and he who remains will die by famine. So I will vent My fury upon them.

Then you will know that I am the LORD, when their slain lie among their idols around their altars, on every high hill, on all the mountaintops, and under every green tree and leafy oak, the places where they offered fragrant incense to all their idols.
I will stretch out My hand against them, and wherever they live I will make the land a desolate waste, from the wilderness to Diblah. Then they will know that I am the LORD.’”

bamot.gloss: High places, elevated shrines on hills and mountaintops used for idolatrous worship, often under sacred trees. Though sometimes tolerated even by faithful kings, they became so associated with Baal worship and syncretism that the prophets condemn them outright; here God vows to demolish them along with their worshipers.

yada_yhwh.gloss: You will know that I am the LORD, a refrain repeated four times in this short chapter. Judgment itself is meant to produce true knowledge of God, not mere information but a recognition of His reality and holiness that idols could never give.

basic.context: For the first time in the book, Ezekiel delivers a spoken oracle rather than only enacting a sign. He turns to face the mountains and hills of Israel, the very landscape where the people built their high places and offered incense to idols under every green tree. God promises to demolish those shrines and to lay the corpses of their worshipers right there among the idols they trusted, so that the land itself will bear witness to what idolatry actually cost.
basic.hermeneutics: This is poetic prophetic judgment speech addressed personified to the land, a common device that intensifies the message without changing its real target, the people who built and used the high places. The chapter should be read for its theological center, that idolatry brings real judgment yet God preserves a remnant who will come to true repentance, rather than mined for geographic detail about which specific hills are meant.
basic.originalLanguages: The oracle targets the bamot, the high places, hilltop shrines that had become synonymous with idol worship in Israel's history. And four times the chapter repeats the refrain yada YHWH, you will know that I am the LORD, showing that the purpose of judgment is not mere destruction but true, undeniable knowledge of God.
basic.typology: The demolished high places anticipate the New Testament's insistence that no place of false worship can stand before the true and living God, and the promised remnant who remember and loathe their sin anticipates the deeper, Spirit-wrought repentance and self-loathing that leads sinners to Christ.
basic.christ: The refrain, that you will know that I am the LORD, finds its fullest answer in Jesus, in whom the invisible God is made fully known, John 1:18, and the loathing self-recognition promised to the exiles anticipates the godly grief that, Paul says, produces repentance leading to salvation, 2 Corinthians 7:10, a grace made possible only through Christ's atoning work.
basic.god: God is a jealous, holy God who will not share His worship with idols, so much so that He turns His judgment against the very hills and shrines that seemed most secure. Yet even in pronouncing total devastation, He deliberately preserves a remnant, showing that His purpose in judgment is ultimately restorative, that His people might truly know Him.
basic.crossReferences: Leviticus 26:30 already threatened that God would cast Israel's corpses on the corpses of their idols, now fulfilled here. Deuteronomy 12:2-3 commanded destroying every high place of Canaanite worship, a command Israel herself came to need. 2 Corinthians 7:10 speaks of godly sorrow leading to repentance, echoing the remnant's loathing here.
basic.oneStory: This is the long-threatened covenant curse finally landing on the very high places where Israel traded her God for idols, yet even in judgment God's purpose is to bring a remnant to true self-knowledge and true knowledge of Him, a pattern of judgment-that-saves fulfilled fully in Christ, who both bears judgment and brings repentance.

context.literary:
The oracle has a clear four part shape. Verses 1 to 7 announce the sword against the high places and the altars, ending on the first 'you will know that I am the LORD.' Verses 8 to 10 turn on the word 'yet': 'Yet I will leave a remnant.' Verses 11 to 12 return to the sentence and widen it, and verses 13 to 14 close by describing the land after the blow and giving the refrain a third and fourth time. The surprise at the centre is that a speech about slaughter makes room for survivors who remember, and the remnant is mentioned before the oracle has finished describing the death.

The address itself is unusual. Ezekiel is told to 'set your face against the mountains of Israel,' 6:2, the same gesture of hostile prophecy later turned on Ammon, 25:2, Sidon, 28:21, and Pharaoh, 29:2. The mountains are told to 'hear the word of the Lord GOD' and are then listed in pairs: mountains and hills, ravines and valleys, 6:3. The list is the geography of Israelite worship, high and low. Every spot where the idols were set up is named, so no corner of the land is spared the sentence.

Idolatry in this chapter is described by what it leaves behind. Altars are smashed, incense stands are cut down, and the bodies of the slain are laid where people prayed, 6:4-5. The word 'idols' returns again and again, and the corpses are set 'before their idols,' 'around their altars,' 'on every high hill,' 6:13, until the whole landscape looks like a graveyard of false worship. There is a deliberate irony in this. The people had gone to the hills to find life and fertility, and they are left lying on them.

Chapter 36 answers this chapter and is easy to miss. Ezekiel will again 'prophesy to the mountains of Israel,' 36:1, and use the same list of mountains, hills, ravines and valleys, 36:4, but this time to promise that they will bear fruit for the people who are coming home, 36:8.
context.historical:
A high place was originally just that: a rise where people sacrificed. Before the temple stood, the people were sacrificing at the high places, 1 Kings 3:2, and the law's problem with them was less their height than their company. The Canaanite sites carried carved images, sacred pillars and Asherah poles, and Israel was told to demolish them, Numbers 33:52 and Deuteronomy 12:2-3. Instead they were rebuilt 'on every high hill and under every green tree,' 1 Kings 14:23, in the north as well, 2 Kings 17:9-11. Hezekiah removed them and even broke the bronze snake of Moses, which had itself become an object of incense, 2 Kings 18:4. Manasseh rebuilt what his father had torn down, 2 Kings 21:3. Josiah, the last great reformer, tore them down from Geba to Beersheba, 2 Kings 23:8, and burned the vessels made for Baal and the host of heaven, 23:4-5. The reform was real and still it did not take root, for Ezekiel is told that the shrines are standing on the eve of exile.

The ancient world thought of mountains as the dwelling of the gods. Canaanite religion tied Baal to a mountain, and the tradition of worship under spreading trees fed on the same instinct: the sacred was found in high places and in shade. Israel's God had chosen one place for His name, Deuteronomy 12:5, and the temptation was to reach for the divine at every convenient hilltop. Prophets saw the cost. Hosea says the daughters turned to prostitution under oak and poplar and terebinth, Hosea 4:13, and the worship was bound up with fertility rites that corrupted the home as well.

The audience also matters. These are exiles sitting in Babylon. The mountains of Israel are far away and they cannot reach them. To hear that the hills they remembered, and perhaps hoped to return to, were under sentence would shatter the idea that a return would simply restore the old arrangement. It also told them why the temple's neighbours had not saved the land.

The last verse sets the limits of the devastation. The BSB reads 'from the wilderness to Diblah,' with a footnote that a few Hebrew manuscripts and the Vulgate have Riblah. Riblah is the city in Syria where Nebuchadnezzar later sat to judge Zedekiah, 2 Kings 25:6, and on that reading the whole land from the southern desert to the northern frontier is covered.
context.canonical:
The refrain 'you will know that I am the LORD' is Ezekiel's signature, but its first great use is the Exodus. God tells Moses that Pharaoh and Israel will know who He is by what He does, Exodus 7:5 and 6:7. Ezekiel's use turns the pattern inward: the God who made Himself known by judging Egypt now makes Himself known by judging His own people, and the knowledge is what the exile must teach.

The law supplies the sentence. Leviticus 26:30 had promised that God would destroy the high places, cut down the incense altars, and 'heap your lifeless bodies on the lifeless remains of your idols.' Ezekiel 6:3-5 is that sentence nearly word for word. Deuteronomy 12:2-3 had commanded the demolition of the high places in the first place, and Israel had finally been made to see what happens to a land that refuses the command.

The prophets keep the picture going. Hosea promises that thorns and thistles will cover the altars of Aven, and that people will cry to the mountains 'Cover us!' and to the hills 'Fall on us!', Hosea 10:8. Jesus quotes that line on the road to the cross, speaking to the weeping women of Jerusalem, Luke 23:28-30, and Revelation hears the same cry from kings and slaves on the great day of wrath, Revelation 6:15-17.

The reversal is already in view in Ezekiel 36, where the mountains of Israel hear a new word, 36:1-8. Behind both stands the promise of a restored worship in which God's own house is the centre of the mountains, Isaiah 2:2-3, and Jesus' word to the Samaritan woman that true worshippers will worship neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem but in spirit and in truth, John 4:21-24. The high places gave way, in the end, not to a better hilltop but to a different kind of temple, one made of people, Ephesians 2:21-22.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel wanted a people cut off from their land to hear something they did not expect: the land was not innocent either. It was easy for exiles to picture the hills at home as a lost paradise, with their altars and groves as part of the good old life. The oracle strips that picture. Those places were where the love of God had been given away, and the sentence on them is a sentence on the love that went there.

He also wanted them to feel the strangeness of the command to clap and stamp, 6:11. The prophet is not asked to remain composed. He is asked to cry 'Alas!' over what God must do. A hearer who has seen the preacher grieve cannot easily take his message as anger alone.

The heart of the passage, though, is in 6:8-10. The exiles were the survivors. They were the ones who had been scattered among the nations and now sat where they were told they would sit. So the oracle has a personal edge: the remembering and the loathing promised in verse 9 are described as something they will do, and the exiles are being told that their present misery is the setting in which that change can begin. Ezekiel's task is to push them toward it by naming idolatry for what it was, adultery against a God who had been grieved, and by promising that when they see the ruin they will 'know' who has been speaking.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This chapter describes a sentence on a specific set of sites and a specific people. It does not say that hills, trees or places of height are evil in themselves, and nothing in the text asks believers to destroy landscapes or other people's shrines. The commands to demolish belonged to Israel under a covenant that fixed its worship at one place and forbade its neighbours' gods in its land, Deuteronomy 12:2-3. The New Testament does not carry that mandate to the church; it carries the underlying principle that God alone is worshipped, 1 John 5:21.

The chapter also describes the inner change God wants in survivors: remembering Him, seeing the grief their idolatry caused Him, and loathing themselves for it, 6:9. That is a description of what God aims at, not a program for producing it. Genuine sorrow cannot be forced, and the New Testament speaks of it as something God grants, Acts 11:18. The practical lesson is that repentance is not a passing feeling but a clear remembering of who God is and what unfaithfulness to Him costs.

The gestures of 6:11 are given to Ezekiel as signs; they are not required for later worshippers. What does carry forward is the willingness to grieve over sin, our own and a nation's, instead of being merely irritated by it, as Jesus did when He wept over Jerusalem, Luke 19:41.

debates.question: In 6:9, who is 'grieved' by the adulterous heart?

views.label: God is the one grieved
views.case: The BSB reads 'how I have been grieved by their adulterous hearts that turned away from Me.' The Hebrew verb at the root is the word for 'break,' so 'I have been broken by their adulterous heart.' On this reading God Himself suffers as the wronged spouse, the thread of Hosea 1 to 3 and Ezekiel 16 carried into this verse. Psalm 78:58 says they enraged Him with their high places and provoked His jealousy.

views.label: God breaks their heart
views.case: Some interpreters read the verb actively: 'I have broken their adulterous heart.' Then the exile itself is God's remedy, breaking the stubborn heart that kept going after idols, and the next clause about their loathing follows naturally as the effect.

views.label: Both ideas at once
views.case: The line can be heard both ways, and the context supports both. The heart that broke Him is the one He must now break, and exile is the point where the two meet.

debates.bearing: The first reading shows a God who feels the injury of betrayal, and the second shows a God who acts to heal it. The passage gives reason to hold both. Whatever the grammar settles, the verse ends the same way: the survivors remember Him and finally see what they did.

debates.question: Is the self-loathing of 6:9 true repentance, or simply knowing God is God?

views.label: Genuine repentance
views.case: The survivors 'remember Me' and 'loathe themselves for the evil they have done,' words that sound like contrition. The same phrase appears in Ezekiel 20:43 and 36:31, where it comes in passages of restoration and a new heart, 36:26-27.

views.label: Recognition without necessarily renewal
views.case: The repeated refrain is that 'you will know,' and in 6:7 and 6:13 that knowledge comes through slaughter. Knowing who God is can be forced by catastrophe without changing the will. In this view 6:9 describes what the survivors will see rather than guaranteeing that every survivor is changed.

views.label: A beginning that God completes
views.case: The loathing is real but not yet the new heart. It prepares the soil. The promise of a heart of flesh, 11:19-20, comes after and is God's own work, so the remnant's remembering opens the door but does not finish the repair.

debates.bearing: The third view fits Ezekiel's overall movement. The exile produces a recognition that God uses, and the renewal of the heart is something He gives. The chapter says what the survivors will feel, and the rest of the book says who makes it last.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter's favorite word for idols, gillulim, appears in 6:4, 6:5, 6:6, 6:9 and 6:13. It is Ezekiel's characteristic term, with most of its occurrences in his book, and it is commonly linked with a word for dung. It is a word of contempt: the false gods are not rivals to God but lumps. The BSB renders it simply 'idols,' and the English loses the sneer. The pairing in 6:5, where Israel's corpses lie before their gillulim, uses the same words as Leviticus 26:30, where God promised to heap 'lifeless bodies on the lifeless remains of your idols.' The idols are as dead as the people who bowed to them.

The address in 6:2 uses the idiom 'set your face against.' It is hostile prophecy, the stance of one who stands before a target and speaks. The same gesture is turned on Ammon, Sidon and Egypt elsewhere in the book, 25:2, 28:21 and 29:2, and its use here on Israel's own mountains puts Israel's land in the place of a foreign enemy.

The heart and the eyes of 6:9 are described with the verb of prostitution, zanah. The people's heart 'went whoring,' the BSB's 'adulterous hearts,' and their eyes 'went whoring after idols,' the BSB's 'eyes that lusted after idols.' It is the language of Hosea, who says a spirit of prostitution has led them astray, Hosea 4:12, and of Jeremiah, who has the people lying down as a prostitute on every high hill, Jeremiah 2:20. Worship is portrayed as a marriage, and idolatry as unfaithfulness in the bedroom of the heart. The verb behind 'grieved,' discussed in the debates above, is a strong one, not a mild regret.

In 6:13 the incense is offered as a 'fragrant,' literally restful or soothing, aroma. The phrase, reyach nichoach, is the standard description of a sacrifice that pleases the LORD, as in Leviticus 1:9. Here it is offered to idols on every hill and under every green tree and leafy oak. Ezekiel borrows the vocabulary of the true altar to describe the false one, and the effect is to make it sound like theft: the people took what belonged to God's worship and spent it elsewhere.

The word 'high place' itself becomes the subject of a pun in Ezekiel 20:29. God asks what the high place, bamah, is that they go to, and the text adds that to this day it is called Bamah. The name is heard as ba, 'go,' and mah, 'what': 'What is this thing you go to?' It is a rhetorical dig at the habit of climbing hills without asking why.

Finally, 6:14 ends with 'Diblah,' with the footnote noting 'Riblah' in the Vulgate and a few manuscripts. The two names differ by a single letter in Hebrew script, an easy slip, and Riblah fits better as a northern boundary.

typology.type: The high places and the mountain of true worship, Ezekiel 6:3
typology.fulfillment: The hilltop shrines were an attempt to meet the divine at a place of one's own choosing. The oracle ends them. Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that the hour is coming when true worshippers will worship the Father neither on 'this mountain' nor in Jerusalem but 'in spirit and in truth,' John 4:21-24. The escalation is from many places to a Person: Jesus Himself is the temple, John 2:19-21, and believers are built into a dwelling for God, Ephesians 2:21-22. The type falls short because the high places were destroyed by the sword while the new worship is established by the gospel, and the first only removes what the second fulfils.

typology.type: 'Fall on us,' the mountains as hiding places, Ezekiel 6:3-5 with Hosea 10:8
typology.fulfillment: The slain are among the idols of the mountains, and Hosea has the survivors crying to the mountains to cover them. On the way to Calvary Jesus tells the daughters of Jerusalem that the days are coming when people will say to the mountains, 'Fall on us!', Luke 23:28-30, and Revelation 6:15-17 sees the whole world say it before the Lamb's wrath. It is a pattern of judgment, repeated and enlarged, not a direct prediction. It falls short of being a gospel, but it shows that the refuge people choose in the last day will be creation itself, which cannot hide them.

typology.type: The adulterous heart and its Husband, Ezekiel 6:9
typology.fulfillment: The image of the unfaithful heart belongs to the marriage picture that runs from Hosea through Ezekiel 16. In the New Testament the picture is brought to rest in Christ, who 'loved the church and gave Himself up for her,' Ephesians 5:25, and Paul fears that believers might be led from a 'simple and pure devotion to Christ,' as a virgin promised to one husband, 2 Corinthians 11:2-3. Israel's Husband was grieved by unfaithfulness; Christ's bride is cleansed and presented in splendor, Ephesians 5:27. The type falls short in that Israel's marriage ended in a divorce of exile, while the Husband in Christ bears the cost of the bride's failure.

typology.type: Mountains that bear fruit again, Ezekiel 6:3 against 36:8
typology.fulfillment: The mountains addressed with a sentence in chapter 6 are addressed again with a promise in chapter 36. Both texts list mountains, hills, ravines and valleys. The land that was stripped will bear branches for the returning people. Hebrews places believers at the end of that journey: 'you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God,' Hebrews 12:22-24, where Jesus mediates a new covenant. The fulfilment goes further than a restored land. The place to which people come is not a hill in Israel but a heavenly city, and Revelation 21 makes it the whole renewed creation.

study.christ:
This oracle never mentions a Messiah, so it leads to Christ along a narrower road than some chapters: by contrast and by consequence. The contrast is between the many places of false worship and the one place where God meets His people. The consequence is what the cross meant for a world of idols.

Begin with the sword. 'I am about to bring a sword against you,' says 6:3, and for the mountains the sword is the army of Babylon. But Scripture knows another time when God's sword is called against a person. 'Awake, O sword, against My Shepherd,' says Zechariah 13:7, and Jesus applies it to Himself on the night of His arrest, Mark 14:27. The judgment pronounced on idolatry in Ezekiel is not softened in the gospel, but it is taken. Paul says Christ became a curse for us, Galatians 3:13, and that God made Him 'to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. The nation that loved idols finally hears the sword; the Son hears it in their place.

Then consider the refrain. 'You will know that I am the LORD' is said here of judgment, and later of restoration. John gives Jesus a refrain of His own. 'When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am He,' John 8:28. The knowledge that Ezekiel's exiles gained from a ruined landscape is given in the gospel from a cross. And Jesus describes eternal life as just this knowledge, 'that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent,' John 17:3.

The high places, finally, are answered by Jesus' body. The temple was the place of God's name, and idolatry in the land had been one long attempt to find a nearer or easier access. Jesus says 'destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,' speaking of His body, John 2:19-21. Worship no longer needs a hill. He takes the place of every altar.

There is also the matter of grief. The God of this oracle is 'grieved' by the adulterous heart, 6:9. Jesus is grieved at the hardness of hearts, Mark 3:5, and weeps over the city that would not come to Him, Luke 19:41. The remnant who remember and loathe themselves have a counterpart in the prodigal who came to his senses, Luke 15:17, though that is an echo, not a prediction.

One caution: the oracle should not be turned into a tidy allegory in which mountains stand for Christ's enemies. Its link to Christ lies in the pattern of judgment and the road from false worship to true knowledge of God, and in the way the New Testament finishes what the exile only begins.
study.god:
The oracle shows a God who will not share His people with anything else. The language of 6:9 is unusually tender for a chapter of sentences: they have turned away from Him, and their eyes have gone after idols. It reads like a spouse speaking of a broken marriage. That is why the punishment is aimed so precisely at the places of the offence. The altars, the incense stands and the bones are all set before the idols, so that the whole landscape will tell the truth about them.

It shows a God who is also sovereign over land and history. He speaks to mountains and ravines as His own creatures and tells them to hear. He brings the sword, and He controls where the slain will fall, near, far or remaining, 6:12. The Babylonian army is not named, because the actor is God: 'I will stretch out My hand against them,' 6:14. The idols, on the other hand, cannot act at all; they are smashed, obliterated and cut down, 6:6. The contrast is the oldest claim of Israel's faith, that the LORD alone is God and the gods are made things, Isaiah 42:8.

It shows a God who keeps His word. 'I did not declare in vain,' says 6:10. The curses of Leviticus 26 had been spoken centuries before, and now they are being met. A God who promises blessing for obedience and curse for betrayal has to mean both, or neither would mean anything. The faithfulness that exiles feared in judgment is the same faithfulness they will lean on when God promises to bring them home.

And it shows mercy inside the sentence. 'Yet I will leave a remnant,' 6:8, interrupts the grim list, and the clause comes first, before the chapter has finished describing the dead. God plans the survivors before He finishes the sword. He wants not the death of the wicked but that they turn, Ezekiel 18:23, and the aim of this oracle, repeated four times, is knowledge, not simply loss.

He is also a God who invites grief. The prophet is told to clap, stamp and cry 'Alas!' at what must happen, 6:11. That is not a God who delights in the sentence. Holiness and sorrow stand together in Him.

For worship, the passage teaches us to guard exclusive loyalty. Idols today are rarely carved; the New Testament names greed as idolatry, Colossians 3:5, and warns that one cannot share the Lord's table with rivals, 1 Corinthians 10:21. The right response to a jealous God is not to resent the demand but to remember what He has been to us, and to let that memory soften the heart before the ruin comes.

crossReferences.note: God promised long before to destroy the high places, cut down the incense altars and heap lifeless bodies on the lifeless remains of idols. Ezekiel 6:3-5 repeats the sentence almost word for word, using the same Hebrew terms for corpses and for idols. The prophet is not adding a threat but reading an old one to people who ignored it.

Israel was told to destroy every place where the nations served their gods, on high mountains, hills and under every green tree, and to smash their altars and pillars. Ezekiel lists the same kind of places, so the demolition Israel had been told to carry out is now carried out on Israel's own shrines.

Josiah desecrated the high places from Geba to Beersheba, the last great attempt to clear the land of them. Reading it beside Ezekiel 6 shows how deep the problem went, since even a thorough reform within living memory did not prevent the oracle.

When Israel entered the land they offered sacrifices on every high hill and leafy tree, and God asks what the high place is to which they go, adding that it is called Bamah to this day. The text plays on the name and fills in the history behind Ezekiel 6: the habit started at the entry to the land.

The mountains of Israel are addressed again, with the same list of mountains, hills, ravines and valleys. This time the word is not a sentence but a promise that they will bear fruit for the people who are coming home. The two chapters stand as a pair, judgment on the land and then its restoration.

The prophet describes worship on mountaintops and under oak, poplar and terebinth, with a spirit of prostitution leading the people astray. It is the same picture as Ezekiel 6:9 and 6:13, and shows that the sin of the high places was seen as both religious and moral unfaithfulness.

The high places will be destroyed and the people will say to the mountains, 'Cover us!' and to the hills, 'Fall on us!' The cry belongs to the same judgment as Ezekiel 6, the moment when the hills that were once trusted become the last refuge. Jesus quotes the cry in Luke 23:30.

Here the restored people 'remember your evil ways and wicked deeds, and you will loathe yourselves for your iniquities and abominations.' It repeats the language of 6:9 and sets it after the gift of a new heart. The loathing that begins in exile is completed in renewal.

On the way to the cross Jesus tells the weeping women to weep for themselves and their children, because the day is coming when people will say to the mountains, 'Fall on us!' He takes the old cry of Hosea 10:8 and Ezekiel's mountains and applies it to the city that is about to reject Him.

Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that true worshippers will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem, but in spirit and in truth. The long contest over which hill is holy ends here, which is where the destruction of the high places in Ezekiel 6 was always meant to lead.

Kings, nobles, the rich and the mighty hide among the rocks and tell the mountains to fall on them, hiding from the wrath of the Lamb. Ezekiel's idolaters lying among their altars on the hills become the pattern of a final day when nothing created can shelter anyone from God.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a God who makes a good world and puts His people in a place where He is near. From Genesis on, the story keeps asking where God may be met and how He may be worshipped. In Eden the answer is simple, and then it breaks. After the fall, people look for the sacred in the wrong places and shape it to their desires. Genesis 11 puts a tower on a plain; Exodus 32 puts a calf at a mountain. Ezekiel 6 is the point where that long drift reaches its limit.

The oracle answers a question raised by every chapter since the entry into the land. Israel was told to clear the high places, and did not. Judges, Kings and the prophets form one long argument, and the argument ends here: if the people will not remove their idols, God will. The land that He gave becomes the place where the covenant curses are carried out. The sentence of Leviticus 26 falls on the exact spots Deuteronomy 12 had named.

But the same chapter carries the seed of recovery. 'Yet I will leave a remnant' is one of the first notes in what becomes the sustained music of the book: a people scattered, a heart recalled, a God who finishes what He begins. By chapter 11 God will promise to be a sanctuary for them in the countries where they live, and will give a new heart, 11:16-20. By chapter 36 the mountains will bear fruit again. The lines of chapter 6 are the dark underside of that hope.

The story comes to rest in Christ. He is the true Israel who worshipped God alone and who faced the temptations on a mountain and refused, Matthew 4:8-10. He bears the sword that falls on idolaters, and He becomes the temple in which God and people meet, John 2:19-21. After Him the question of the right mountain is closed, John 4:21-24, and the Spirit is poured out on a people who are themselves God's house, 1 Corinthians 3:16.

The new creation fulfils it. In Revelation 21 there is no temple in the city, because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple, 21:22. No shrine is needed on a hill, because God's presence fills everything, and nothing impure will enter the city, 21:27. The people who once climbed hills in search of life have what the hills could never give, and idols are gone for good.

quiz.q: What does God command Ezekiel to prophesy against in this chapter?

options.text: The king of Babylon and his armies.
options.note: The oracle targets Israel's own high places, not Babylon's king.

options.text: The mountains, hills, ravines, and valleys of Israel, and the high places built on them.
options.note: Ezekiel 6:2-3 addresses the land and its idolatrous shrines directly.

options.text: The temple in Jerusalem specifically.
options.note: The focus here is the countryside high places, not the temple building.

options.text: Nothing in particular; the oracle has no clear target.
options.note: The mountains and their idolatrous shrines are named explicitly.

quiz.q: What will happen to the corpses of the slain according to this oracle?

options.text: They will be carried to Babylon for burial.
options.note: The bodies are pictured lying at the high places themselves.

options.text: There will be no slain at all.
options.note: The chapter emphasizes widespread slaughter among the idols.

options.text: They will fall and lie before the very idols the people worshiped.
options.note: Ezekiel 6:4-5 and 6:13 describe corpses lying among their idols and altars.

options.text: They will be given honorable burial in Jerusalem.
options.note: The oracle pictures dishonorable exposure, not honorable burial.

quiz.q: What promise does God make even within this harsh judgment oracle?

options.text: He promises that no one will survive at all.
options.note: The opposite; a remnant is explicitly preserved.

options.text: He promises immediate restoration of the temple.
options.note: No such immediate restoration is promised in this chapter.

options.text: He makes no promise of any kind.
options.note: The remnant promise is stated clearly in verses 8-9.

options.text: He will leave a remnant who escape and are scattered among the nations.
options.note: Ezekiel 6:8-9 promises survivors who will remember and loathe their sin.

quiz.q: What will the surviving remnant come to feel about their past idolatry?

options.text: They will loathe themselves for their evil and abominations.
options.note: Ezekiel 6:9 describes this self-loathing response to remembering God.

options.text: They will feel nothing at all.
options.note: A strong emotional and moral response is described.

options.text: They will feel proud of their former worship.
options.note: The text describes loathing and grief, not pride.

options.text: They will blame God entirely for their circumstances.
options.note: The loathing is directed at their own evil and abominations, not at God.

quiz.q: What refrain is repeated throughout this chapter to explain the purpose of judgment?

options.text: Then they will forget that I am the LORD.
options.note: The refrain is about coming to know God, the opposite of forgetting.

options.text: Then the nations will rejoice.
options.note: No such refrain about the nations rejoicing appears here.

options.text: Then they will know that I am the LORD.
options.note: This exact refrain occurs four times across the chapter.

options.text: No refrain is repeated in this chapter.
options.note: The knowledge-of-the-LORD refrain is a defining feature of the passage.

questions: The high places felt safe and familiar to Israel, yet they were exactly what God judged. What familiar, comfortable habits or attachments in your own life might be quietly competing with true worship of God?
God repeats 'then you will know that I am the LORD' four times in this short chapter. Where in your own story has hardship or loss led you to know God more truly, not just know facts about Him?
The remnant's repentance began with remembering God and loathing their own sin, not with excusing it. How comfortable are you with genuine, specific sorrow over sin rather than vague, general guilt?
God's judgment on the high places was thorough, reaching every hill and green tree. Is there an area of compromise in your life you have been unwilling to let God thoroughly address?

Even in devastating judgment, God's purpose was ultimately a remnant restored to true knowledge of Him. How does trusting God's good purposes change the way you endure a season of discipline or hardship?

translationNotes.note: The high places, translated bamot in Hebrew, were elevated open-air shrines, often on hilltops or under sacred trees, associated throughout Israel's history with syncretistic and idolatrous worship.
The phrase describing adulterous hearts and lusting eyes uses covenant marriage imagery common in the prophets, picturing idolatry as spiritual unfaithfulness to a husband, here God Himself.

Diblah, marking the northern extent of the desolation, is generally understood to be a scribal or textual variant for Riblah, a location further north in Syria used as a staging point by Babylonian forces.
